passages.title: The Branch Line
passages.text:
When I was a boy the branch line still ran, and the little station at Harleigh was the centre of my summer world. Each morning I would walk down through the lane, past the blackberry hedges, to lean on the white fence and wait for the half-past-nine train to come sighing round the bend. I loved the ritual of it: the stationmaster, Mr Pettifer, polishing the brass lamps until they burned like small suns; the porter wheeling his barrow of milk churns that rang like dull bells as they knocked together. Nothing was hurried there. The whole place seemed to keep the slow, contented time of the fields around it.

When the train did arrive it was never quite the monster the picture books had promised. It puffed in almost apologetically, breathing steam over the platform, and I would stand as close as I dared, drinking in the warm smell of oil and coal-smoke that clung to my clothes for the rest of the day. Mr Pettifer knew every passenger by name. He would ask after their gardens and their grandmothers, and hold the train an extra minute if old Mrs Dacre was seen hurrying up the lane with her basket. To wait for a train, in those days, was not to waste time but to spend it, unhurried, among people who had all the time in the world.

They closed the line the year I turned fifteen. The rails were lifted, the little station boarded up, and the brass lamps sold. I went back once, years afterwards, and found the platform swallowed by nettles and the fence long gone. Yet I confess I would not trade those slow mornings for all the swift, silent journeys of today. Something went out of the country when the branch lines died, and no timetable has ever brought it back.

passages.title: Bring Back the Line
passages.text:
You may think of a closed railway line as a thing safely buried in the past, but I want to persuade you that it is nothing of the sort. Across the country lie hundreds of miles of old track-bed, cleared long ago and never built upon, waiting quietly to be useful again. Reopening even a fraction of them would be one of the wisest investments a town could make, and the case is far stronger than most people suppose.

Consider the figures. A recent study found that towns cut off from the rail network in the last century have, on average, grown more slowly and seen fewer new businesses than their connected neighbours. Where a line has been restored, the effect is measurable within a decade: house prices steady, shops reopen, and young people who would once have moved away find reasons to stay. A road cannot do this, for a road merely lets people pass through; a station gives them a reason to stop.

There are those who object that the cost is too great, and I do not pretend it is small. But weigh it against the alternative. Every year we spend more on widening motorways that are congested again almost as soon as they open. A railway carries far more people on far less land, and it does so without pouring fumes into the air our children breathe. If we are serious about the future, we cannot keep treating the railway as a relic. The track-bed is still there. The question is not whether we can afford to rebuild the line, but whether we can afford not to.

questions.stem: What impression do we get of the narrator's feelings about his boyhood, judging by how he describes the station?

options.text: He found it dull and longed to leave for a bigger town
He treasured it and remembers it with deep affection
He was frightened of the trains and kept his distance
He was mainly interested in earning money as a porter
He thought the villagers foolish for moving so slowly

questions.explanation: The loving detail ('the centre of my summer world', 'I loved the ritual of it') shows deep affection, not boredom or fear.

questions.stem: According to Text 1, what did the stationmaster polish until it shone?

options.text: The milk churns
The white fence
The barrow
The brass lamps
The platform floor

questions.explanation: Mr Pettifer is described 'polishing the brass lamps until they burned like small suns'.

questions.stem: In Text 1, the narrator says he loved 'the ritual of it'. What does 'ritual' mean here?

options.text: A religious ceremony held at the station
A sudden and surprising event
A strict rule the villagers were forced to obey
A game the children invented
A set of familiar actions repeated each day

questions.explanation: A 'ritual' here is the comforting, familiar sequence of daily happenings he lists after the word.

questions.stem: Why does the writer include the detail that Mr Pettifer would hold the train an extra minute for a passenger hurrying up the lane?

options.text: To show that the trains were often faulty and late
To prove the stationmaster was breaking the rules
To illustrate the unhurried, personal character of the place
To explain why the line was eventually closed
To warn the reader against relying on the railway

questions.explanation: The held minute is an example of the passage's main idea: an unhurried world where people mattered more than the timetable.

questions.stem: What device does the writer use in the phrase 'burned like small suns'?

options.text: Simile
Metaphor
Personification
Onomatopoeia
Alliteration

questions.explanation: The lamps are compared to suns using 'like', which makes it a simile.

questions.stem: What can we infer about the pace of life in the village around the station?

options.text: It was tense and competitive
It was slow and easy-going
It was dangerous and unpredictable
It was busy and industrial
It was lonely and joyless

questions.explanation: Phrases like 'the slow, contented time of the fields' and 'people who had all the time in the world' show an easy-going pace.

questions.stem: How old was the narrator when the line was closed?

options.text: Nine
Twelve
Eighteen
Twenty
Fifteen

questions.explanation: The text states 'They closed the line the year I turned fifteen'.

questions.stem: The narrator says the platform was 'swallowed by nettles'. What is the effect of describing the nettles this way?

options.text: It suggests the nettles were good to eat
It makes the station's decay seem gradual and gentle
It gives a sense of nature swiftly overwhelming what people made
It shows the narrator was afraid of the plants
It proves the station was rebuilt soon afterwards

questions.explanation: 'Swallowed' pictures the plants consuming the platform, giving a vivid sense of nature overwhelming the abandoned station.

questions.stem: How would you best describe the tone of the final paragraph of Text 1?

options.text: Angry and accusing
Wistful and regretful
Cheerful and light-hearted
Cold and factual
Anxious and fearful

questions.explanation: Lines such as 'I would not trade those slow mornings' and 'something went out of the country' create a wistful, regretful tone.

questions.stem: In the third paragraph of Text 2, the writer states an objection ('the cost is too great') before answering it. Why does the writer structure the argument this way?

options.text: To admit that the objection cannot be answered
To fill space because there was little left to say
To show fairness and then dismantle the objection, making the argument more convincing
To change the subject away from railways
To confuse a reader who disagrees

questions.explanation: Raising and then answering the strongest objection makes the writer appear reasonable and strengthens the persuasion.

questions.stem: Which quotation from Text 2 best supports the idea that a station does more for a town than a road does?

options.text: 'the track-bed is still there'
'I do not pretend it is small'
'hundreds of miles of old track-bed'
'congested again almost as soon as they open'
'a road merely lets people pass through; a station gives them a reason to stop'

questions.explanation: This contrast between passing through and stopping is the exact evidence that a station benefits a town in a way a road does not.

questions.stem: In the phrase 'treating the railway as a relic', what does the word 'relic' suggest about the railway?

options.text: a valuable treasure to be guarded
a dangerous machine
a leftover from the past with no use today
a brand-new invention
a place of worship

questions.explanation: The writer argues the railway is NOT a mere leftover of the past but useful now, so 'relic' means an outdated survival.

questions.stem: According to the study mentioned in Text 2, how have towns cut off from the rail network fared compared with connected towns?

options.text: They have grown more slowly and seen fewer new businesses
They have grown faster and gained more businesses
They have kept exactly the same rate of growth
They have lost all of their shops within a year
They have built more motorways instead

questions.explanation: The passage reports such towns 'have, on average, grown more slowly and seen fewer new businesses than their connected neighbours'.

questions.stem: The writer ends Text 2 by saying the real question is 'whether we can afford not to'. What is the writer trying to make the reader feel?

options.text: That rebuilding is an impossible dream
That doing nothing is the truly costly choice
That the reader should decide the matter is unimportant
That railways are too expensive to consider
That roads are always the better option

questions.explanation: By flipping the usual worry about cost, the writer presses the reader to feel that NOT rebuilding is what they cannot afford.

questions.stem: What can we infer about the readers Text 2 is chiefly aimed at?

options.text: People who have already reopened their local line
Railway engineers who need technical instructions
Children learning to read a timetable
People who dislike living in towns altogether
People who currently doubt that reopening lines is worthwhile

questions.explanation: The piece opens by tackling readers who think a closed line is 'safely buried in the past', so it targets doubters it wants to persuade.

questions.stem: What subject do both Text 1 and Text 2 concern themselves with?

options.text: The building of new motorways
The growing of blackberries
The polishing of brass
The teaching of village children
Railways and railway lines

questions.explanation: Both texts are about railways: Text 1 remembers a branch line, Text 2 argues for reopening closed lines.

questions.stem: Which best describes the difference in tone between the two texts?

options.text: The memoir is nostalgic, whereas the persuasive piece is urgent
The memoir is angry, whereas the persuasive piece is amused
The memoir is fearful, whereas the persuasive piece is wistful
Both are equally light-hearted from beginning to end
The memoir is coldly technical, whereas the persuasive piece is playful

questions.explanation: Text 1 fondly remembers the past (nostalgic); Text 2 tries to win the reader round to an argument (persuasive).

questions.stem: In terms of time, how do the two texts differ in what they mainly look towards?

options.text: The first looks back to a vanished past; the second looks ahead to what could be built
The first looks ahead to what could be built; the second looks back to a vanished past
Both dwell only on the present day
The first ignores time altogether, while the second dwells on it
Both fix their gaze only on what is still to come

questions.explanation: Text 1 is a memory of boyhood ('When I was a boy'); Text 2 argues about what a town should do next ('the future').

questions.stem: How do the two writers mainly support what they say?

options.text: Both lean on scientific statistics
One writer leans on figures, while the other leans on personal memories
Both lean only on interviews with passengers
One writer leans on personal memories, while the other leans on figures and reasoning
Neither writer offers any support at all

questions.explanation: Text 1's support is remembered sensory detail; Text 2's support is a study, figures and step-by-step argument.

questions.stem: How does each writer's relationship with the reader differ?

options.text: The narrator directly instructs the reader, while the campaigner holds the reader at a distance
Both give the reader orders throughout
Neither ever mentions or addresses the reader
The narrator shares a private recollection, while the campaigner appeals straight to the reader to win them round
The narrator argues with the reader, while the campaigner tells a bedtime story

questions.explanation: Text 1 recounts a personal memory ('I would walk down'); Text 2 repeatedly addresses 'you' to persuade.

questions.stem: In what way do both writers ultimately agree about the railway?

options.text: Both think the railway was better replaced by roads
Both believe railways should never have been built
Both regard the loss of railway lines as something to be lamented or reversed
Both think railways are dangerous and dirty
Both feel the railway made villages grow too fast

questions.explanation: Text 1 mourns what was lost when the line closed; Text 2 wants such lines rebuilt. Both value the railway.

questions.stem: Within Text 1, why does the writer include the second paragraph (beginning 'When the train did arrive')?

options.text: To describe the train's arrival and the stationmaster's personal care for passengers
To warn the reader that the trains were dangerous
To list the reasons the branch line was later closed
To argue that modern journeys are better than the old ones
To explain how the railway was built in the first place

questions.explanation: The paragraph pictures the train puffing in and Mr Pettifer knowing every passenger by name, holding the train for Mrs Dacre.

questions.stem: How is each text organised?

options.text: Both are laid out as a list of instructions
The recollection is built as a step-by-step case; the appeal unfolds as a tale moving through time
Both are laid out as a series of poems
The recollection unfolds as a tale moving through time; the appeal is built as a step-by-step case
Both jump about with no order at all

questions.explanation: Text 1 moves from boyhood to closure to a return visit (a story in time); Text 2 sets out a claim, evidence and answered objection (an argument).

questions.stem: According to Text 2, what advantage does a railway have over a widened motorway?

options.text: It is always cheaper to build than a road
It never needs any repair once it is built
It allows lorries to travel faster between towns
It carries far more people on far less land, and without adding fumes to the air
It removes the need for towns to have any shops

questions.explanation: The writer states a railway 'carries far more people on far less land, and it does so without pouring fumes into the air our children breathe'.

questions.stem: In Text 1 the writer says the train 'puffed in almost apologetically'. Which device is this?

options.text: Simile
Personification
Rhyme
Exaggeration
Repetition

questions.explanation: Giving the train the human quality of behaving 'apologetically' is personification.
